title: Trump wants a made-for-TV summit – but Kim Jong-un will decide the ratings
gist: With his approval near record lows before the 2026 US midterms and the Iran war a liability, Trump is reviving North Korea summitry as a controllable televised 'peacemaker' win; but Kim Jong-un, now backed by Russia and China, holds the leverage and can wait Washington out.

themes.theme: Domestic drivers of the summit push

insights.claim: Trump's approval sits at 33% — one point lower than his previous record low in the week after the 6 January insurrection — with popularity for his Iran war and his leadership hovering in the low 30s ahead of the 2026 midterms.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Record-low approval before midterms is the mechanism pushing Trump toward a low-substance, high-visibility diplomatic event — a signal for volatility in North Korea policy.
insights.quote: Trump’s own approval sits at 33%, one point lower than Trump’s previous record in the week after the 6 January insurrection
insights.locator: In such a referendum, Trump’s popularity is important

insights.claim: In the past two weeks Trump abruptly cut back joint exercises with South Korea, floated another Kim summit, and repeated that only his personal relationship with Kim can pull North Korea back from the brink.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Cutting exercises as a summit overture concedes leverage before talks begin — watch for further unilateral concessions timed to the campaign calendar.

insights.claim: The author frames a new Kim summit as an 'aesthetic victory' Trump can control — a televised advertorial for his self-image as peacemaker — as the opportunity for substantive foreign-policy success becomes scarce.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Treating diplomacy as campaign advertising means optics over outcomes — expect spectacle without denuclearisation deliverables.
insights.quote: A new summit with Kim offers Trump an aesthetic victory that he can control – a televised ad for his vision of himself as peacemaker
insights.locator: The political value of a visible diplomatic success

insights.claim: The war in Iran, which Trump imagined would be swift, has bogged down his foreign agenda into 'an oily albatross,' imposing daily political and economic costs, while Ukraine and Gaza remain unresolved.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: A grinding Iran war raises the political premium on a quick North Korea 'win' — a driver of erratic diplomatic timing.
insights.quote: the war in Iran has bogged Trump’s foreign agenda and become an oily albatross around his neck
insights.locator: Trump had imagined a war in Iran to be swift

insights.claim: The author asserts the US replaced Venezuela's kidnapped president with an equally brutal leader whose main change was to send oil revenues northward to the United States.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Signals the author's read that recent US interventions are transactional and oil-driven — context for judging the North Korea play.
insights.locator: Trump had imagined a war in Iran to be swift

insights.claim: Kim's partnership with Russia — underwritten by North Korean troops on Ukraine's frontline — has enabled financial workarounds that render inert many Western sanctions, while China has restored trade and expanded cooperation.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Sanctions leverage has eroded, weakening US ability to extract concessions — a structural shift against Washington in any negotiation.
insights.quote: new financial workarounds that have rendered inert many of the Western sanctions against the North Korean regime
insights.locator: In the eight years since that summit

insights.claim: The power dynamic has inverted since 2018: where Kim then needed something from Trump, in 2026 it is Trump who needs Kim to participate in the spectacle.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Inverted leverage means any deal likely favours Pyongyang — watch for US acceptance of North Korea's nuclear status as the price of a photo-op.
insights.quote: In 2018, Kim needed something of Trump. In 2026, Trump needs Kim to participate in the spectacle.

insights.claim: Pyongyang is signalling it wants the US to accept its status as a nuclear power and to reduce South Korea's capacity to call on American military support.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Formal US recognition of a nuclear North Korea and looser US-ROK ties would reset East Asian security assumptions — a tail risk for regional allies.
insights.quote: Pyongyang is signalling that it wants the US to accept its status as a nuclear power

insights.claim: After the 2018 Singapore summit 46% of Americans said it made Trump look stronger — helping Republicans defy odds and gain two Senate seats — yet 38% said North Korea gained more, showing voters simultaneously judged Kim got the better deal and Trump looked stronger.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Precedent that summit theatre can pay electoral dividends regardless of substance — explains why the tactic is being repeated.
insights.quote: They thought that North Korea got the better deal and that Trump looked stronger.

insights.claim: Journalist Aslı Aydıntaşbaş told Reuters that adversaries understand Trump's 'political clock is shorter than theirs' and can wait for Washington to lose patience and strike a more favourable deal.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: The 'shorter political clock' is a reusable lens for pricing US negotiating weakness across adversaries, not just North Korea.
insights.quote: adversaries understand that Trump’s “political clock is shorter than theirs”
insights.locator: As the Turkish journalist Aslı Aydıntaşbaş told Reuters
